title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Submodular Reward
claim: Agents with overlapping coverage yield diminishing marginal returns, so adding a team member helps less than the sum of individual contributions.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, arrow between; dashed ellipses show overlapping coverage
description: Two framed panels are joined by a black arrow that points from left to right. The left panel has one quadruped robot with a mechanical arm on the right side. A dashed gray ellipse around it shades the nearby boxes, which look faded because they are covered. The other brown boxes are scattered outside the ellipse. The right panel adds a second robot at the top center, with a dashed green-tinted ellipse around the boxes near it. The two ellipses overlap, and a box in the overlap is shaded by both. Isometric brown box icons stand for targets or tasks. The picture shows that the second agent covers new boxes but also overlaps with the first, so its marginal gain is smaller. The eye goes first to the robots and the overlapping ellipses.
caption: Demonstration of multi-agent collaboration.
abstract: In this paper, we study cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) where the joint reward exhibits submodularity, which is a natural property capturing diminishing marginal returns when adding agents to a team. Unlike standard MARL with additive rewards, submodular rewards model realistic scenarios where agent contributions overlap (e.g., multi-drone surveillance, collaborative exploration). We provide the first formal framework for this setting and develop algorithms with provable guarantees on sample efficiency and regret bound. For known dynamics, our greedy policy optimization achieves a $1/2$-approximation with polynomial complexity in the number of agents $K$, overcoming the exponential curse of dimensionality inherent in joint policy optimization. For unknown dynamics, we propose a UCB-based learning algorithm achieving a $1/2$-regret of $O(H^2KS\sqrt{AT})$ over $T$ episodes.
